claim: Lysine 27-to-methionine (K27M) mutations in the H3.1 or H3.3 histone genes are characteristic of pediatric diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs).
source: Lysine 27-to-methionine (K27M) mutations in the H3.1 or H3.3 histone genes are characteristic of pediatric diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the citations in the introduction section.

claim: K27M oncohistone mutations dominantly inhibit histone H3K27 trimethylation and silencing.
source: These oncohistone mutations dominantly inhibit histone H3K27 trimethylation and silencing, but it is unknown how oncohistone type affects gliomagenesis.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the introduction and by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The genomic distributions of H3.1 and H3.3 oncohistones in human patient-derived DMG cells are consistent with DNA replication-coupled deposition of histone H3.1.
source: We show that the genomic distributions of H3.1 and H3.3 oncohistones in human patient-derived DMG cells are consistent with the DNAreplication-coupled deposition of histone H3.1 and the predominant replication-independent deposition of histone H3.3.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling data showing uniform distribution of H3.1K27M across the genome (Figure 3C, 3E).

claim: The genomic distributions of H3.1 and H3.3 oncohistones in human patient-derived DMG cells are consistent with predominant replication-independent deposition of histone H3.3.
source: We show that the genomic distributions of H3.1 and H3.3 oncohistones in human patient-derived DMG cells are consistent with the DNAreplication-coupled deposition of histone H3.1 and the predominant replication-independent deposition of histone H3.3.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling data showing H3.3K27M enrichment at active promoters (Figure 3E) and at sites of H3K4me2 (Supplementary file 1).

claim: H3K27 trimethylation is reduced for both H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M oncohistone types.
source: Although H3K27 trimethylation is reduced for both oncohistone types, H3.3K27M-bearing cells retain some domains, and only H3.1K27M-bearing cells lack H3K27 trimethylation.
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting (Figure 3A) and CUT&RUN profiling data (Figure 4A).

claim: H3.3K27M-bearing cells retain some H3K27me3 domains.
source: Although H3K27 trimethylation is reduced for both oncohistone types, H3.3K27M-bearing cells retain some domains, and only H3.1K27M-bearing cells lack H3K27 trimethylation.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling showing H3K27me3 domains in Clusters III and IV in H3.3K27M cells (Figure 4A).

claim: Only H3.1K27M-bearing cells lack H3K27 trimethylation.
source: Although H3K27 trimethylation is reduced for both oncohistone types, H3.3K27M-bearing cells retain some domains, and only H3.1K27M-bearing cells lack H3K27 trimethylation.
evidence: This is supported by spike-in normalized CUT&RUN data showing very low H3K27me3 levels in H3.1K27M cells (Figure 3C, Figure 5B).

claim: Neither H3.1K27M nor H3.3K27M oncohistones interfere with PRC2 binding to chromatin.
source: Neither oncohistone interferes with PRC2 binding.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling of SUZ12 and MTF2 showing similar enrichment at H3K27me3 domains in all cell lines (Figure 5A, 5B).

claim: Inhibition of H3K27 trimethylation occurs only when H3K27M oncohistones are deposited into chromatin.
source: Using Drosophila as a model, we demonstrate that inhibition of H3K27 trimethylation occurs only when H3K27M oncohistones are deposited into chromatin and only when expressed in cycling cells.
evidence: This is supported by Drosophila S2 cell experiments showing that H3 tail fusion proteins lacking histone fold domains do not inhibit H3K27me3 (Figure 1A, 1B).

claim: Inhibition of H3K27 trimethylation by H3K27M oncohistones occurs only when expressed in cycling cells.
source: Using Drosophila as a model, we demonstrate that inhibition of H3K27 trimethylation occurs only when H3K27M oncohistones are deposited into chromatin and only when expressed in cycling cells.
evidence: This is supported by Drosophila eye disc experiments showing that H3.3K27M does not inhibit H3K27me3 when co-expressed with p21 cell cycle inhibitor (Figure 2L, 2M).

claim: Oncohistones inhibit the H3K27 methyltransferase as chromatin patterns are being duplicated in proliferating cells, predisposing them to tumorigenesis.
source: We propose that oncohistones inhibit the H3K27 methyltransferase as chromatin patterns are being duplicated in proliferating cells, predisposing them to tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs) are lethal pediatric brain tumors.
source: Diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs) are lethal pediatric brain tumors associated with mutations in genes encoding either histone H3.1 or H3.3, most frequently the lysine 27-to-methionine (H3K27M) 'oncohistone' substitutions (Schwartzentruber et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: DMGs are associated with mutations in genes encoding either histone H3.1 or H3.3, most frequently the lysine 27-to-methionine (H3K27M) substitutions.
source: Diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs) are lethal pediatric brain tumors associated with mutations in genes encoding either histone H3.1 or H3.3, most frequently the lysine 27-to-methionine (H3K27M) 'oncohistone' substitutions (Schwartzentruber et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: H3K27M oncohistones cause the global reduction of histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3).
source: H3K27M oncohistones cause the global reduction of histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3), a covalent modification that marks silenced regions in the genome.
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data (Figure 3A) and CUT&RUN profiling data (Figure 4A).

claim: H3K27me3 is a covalent modification that marks silenced regions in the genome.
source: H3K27M oncohistones cause the global reduction of histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3), a covalent modification that marks silenced regions in the genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of epigenetics.

claim: H3K27M oncohistones comprise only ~5–15% of the total H3 histone within DMG cells.
source: Since H3K27M oncohistones comprise only ~5–15% of the total H3 histone within DMG cells (Chan et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2013), they are thought to dominantly inhibit the H3K27 methyltransferase Enhancer of Zeste Homologue-2 (EZH2).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: H3K27M oncohistones are thought to dominantly inhibit the H3K27 methyltransferase Enhancer of Zeste Homologue-2 (EZH2).
source: Since H3K27M oncohistones comprise only ~5–15% of the total H3 histone within DMG cells (Chan et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2013), they are thought to dominantly inhibit the H3K27 methyltransferase Enhancer of Zeste Homologue-2 (EZH2).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: An H3K27M peptide binds in the active site of EZH2 and inhibits catalytic activity in vitro.
source: Indeed, an H3K27M peptide binds in the active site of EZH2 and inhibits catalytic activity in vitro, and ectopic expression of either oncohistone inhibits H3K27 methylation in vivo (Chan et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2013; Bender et al., 2013; Justin et al., 2016; Stafford et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Ectopic expression of either H3.1K27M or H3.3K27M oncohistone inhibits H3K27 methylation in vivo.
source: Indeed, an H3K27M peptide binds in the active site of EZH2 and inhibits catalytic activity in vitro, and ectopic expression of either oncohistone inhibits H3K27 methylation in vivo (Chan et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2013; Bender et al., 2013; Justin et al., 2016; Stafford et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and experimental data in Drosophila (Figure 1A, 1B).

claim: Oncohistones inhibit Polycomb-mediated repression of oncogenes, predisposing cells to tumorigenesis.
source: These studies have led to the hypothesis that oncohistones inhibit Polycomb-mediated repression of oncogenes, predisposing cells to tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited literature.

claim: Most DMG patients carry K27M mutations in the genes encoding the histone variant H3.3.
source: Most DMG patients carry K27M mutations in the genes encoding the histone variant H3.3, and only ~20% of mutations are in histone H3.1 genes (Wu et al., 2012; Fontebasso et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Only ~20% of K27M mutations in DMG patients are in histone H3.1 genes.
source: Most DMG patients carry K27M mutations in the genes encoding the histone variant H3.3, and only ~20% of mutations are in histone H3.1 genes (Wu et al., 2012; Fontebasso et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: There are only two genes encoding H3.3 in the human genome.
source: This ratio is surprising given that there are only two genes encoding H3.3 and 12 genes encoding H3.1 in the human genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the human genome.

claim: There are 12 genes encoding H3.1 in the human genome.
source: This ratio is surprising given that there are only two genes encoding H3.3 and 12 genes encoding H3.1 in the human genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the human genome.

claim: H3.3 or H3.1 K27M mutations are associated with distinct sets of secondary mutations in cancers.
source: In addition, although these two histones are very similar, H3.3 or H3.1 K27M mutations are associated with distinct sets of secondary mutations in cancers, and H3.1 mutations are associated with earlier onset gliomagenesis.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and genotyping data (Supplementary file 5).

claim: H3.1 K27M mutations are associated with earlier onset gliomagenesis.
source: In addition, although these two histones are very similar, H3.3 or H3.1 K27M mutations are associated with distinct sets of secondary mutations in cancers, and H3.1 mutations are associated with earlier onset gliomagenesis.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: H3.3 K27M mutations are restricted to gliomas.
source: Finally, while the H3.3 mutations are restricted to gliomas, H3.1 mutations have also been identified in AML and melanomas (Mackay et al., 2017; Nacev et al., 2019; Lehnertz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: H3.1 K27M mutations have been identified in AML and melanomas.
source: Finally, while the H3.3 mutations are restricted to gliomas, H3.1 mutations have also been identified in AML and melanomas (Mackay et al., 2017; Nacev et al., 2019; Lehnertz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The two oncohistones differ in tumorigenic effects.
source: These differences suggest that the two oncohistones differ in tumorigenic effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences in secondary mutations and cancer types associated with each oncohistone.

claim: Both H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M oncohistones require cell cycle progression in order to inhibit EZH2.
source: Studies in mammalian cells suggest that both H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M oncohistones require cell cycle progression in order to inhibit EZH2 (Chan et al., 2013; Nagaraja et al., 2019), although the etiology of this dependency remains unknown.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and experimental data in Drosophila (Figure 2L, 2M).

claim: Histone H3.1 is massively produced only in S phase of the cell cycle.
source: Histone H3.1 is massively produced only in S phase of the cell cycle, but histone H3.3 is produced constitutively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about histone biology.

claim: Histone H3.3 is produced constitutively.
source: Histone H3.1 is massively produced only in S phase of the cell cycle, but histone H3.3 is produced constitutively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about histone biology.

claim: The bulk of histone deposition occurs during DNA replication as new chromatin is assembled.
source: While the bulk of histone deposition occurs during DNA replication as new chromatin is assembled, the H3.3 histone is deposited both during DNA replication and at sites of active histone turnover, and these are evolutionarily conserved properties of the two histone types (Ahmad and Henikoff, 2002; Tagami et al., 2004; Drané et al., 2010; Ray-Gallet et al., 2011; Clément et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: The H3.3 histone is deposited both during DNA replication and at sites of active histone turnover.
source: While the bulk of histone deposition occurs during DNA replication as new chromatin is assembled, the H3.3 histone is deposited both during DNA replication and at sites of active histone turnover, and these are evolutionarily conserved properties of the two histone types (Ahmad and Henikoff, 2002; Tagami et al., 2004; Drané et al., 2010; Ray-Gallet et al., 2011; Clément et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature and experimental data (Figure 3E).

claim: The deposition properties of H3.1 and H3.3 are evolutionarily conserved.
source: While the bulk of histone deposition occurs during DNA replication as new chromatin is assembled, the H3.3 histone is deposited both during DNA replication and at sites of active histone turnover, and these are evolutionarily conserved properties of the two histone types (Ahmad and Henikoff, 2002; Tagami et al., 2004; Drané et al., 2010; Ray-Gallet et al., 2011; Clément et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and the use of Drosophila as a model system.

claim: Overexpressing either H3.2K27M or H3.3K27M oncohistone inhibits H3K27 methylation only in cells progressing through S-phase.
source: Capitalizing on this conservation, we use Drosophila to show that overexpressing either H3K27M oncohistone inhibits H3K27 methylation only in cells progressing through S-phase and only if deposited into chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by Drosophila eye disc experiments with p21 co-expression (Figure 2L, 2M).

claim: Overexpressing either H3.2K27M or H3.3K27M oncohistone inhibits H3K27 methylation only if deposited into chromatin.
source: Capitalizing on this conservation, we use Drosophila to show that overexpressing either H3K27M oncohistone inhibits H3K27 methylation only in cells progressing through S-phase and only if deposited into chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by Drosophila S2 cell experiments with histone tail constructs (Figure 1A, 1B).

claim: The H3.1 K27M oncohistone is distributed across the genome, consistent with replication-coupled deposition.
source: We demonstrate that the H3.1 K27M oncohistone is distributed across the genome, consistent with replication-coupled deposition, and these cells have very low H3K27 methylation throughout the genome.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling data showing uniform distribution (Figure 3C, 3E).

claim: H3.1K27M-bearing cells have very low H3K27 methylation throughout the genome.
source: We demonstrate that the H3.1 K27M oncohistone is distributed across the genome, consistent with replication-coupled deposition, and these cells have very low H3K27 methylation throughout the genome.
evidence: This is supported by spike-in normalized CUT&RUN data (Figure 3C, Figure 5B).

claim: The bulk of H3.3 K27M oncohistone localizes to sites of active histone turnover.
source: In contrast, the bulk of H3.3 K27M oncohistone localizes to sites of active histone turnover, although we also detect the oncohistone at a low level genome-wide, which is consistent with H3.3 deposition during DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling showing enrichment at active promoters (Figure 3E) and correlation with H3K4me2 (Supplementary file 1).

claim: H3.3 K27M oncohistone is detected at a low level genome-wide, which is consistent with H3.3 deposition during DNA replication.
source: In contrast, the bulk of H3.3 K27M oncohistone localizes to sites of active histone turnover, although we also detect the oncohistone at a low level genome-wide, which is consistent with H3.3 deposition during DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling showing moderate genome-wide signal (Figure 3C).

claim: H3.3K27M-bearing cells have low global levels of H3K27 methylation but retain high level methylation at a small number of domains.
source: While H3.3K27M-bearing cells have low global levels of H3K27 methylation, they retain high level methylation at a small number of domains.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling showing H3K27me3 domains in Clusters III and IV (Figure 4A).

claim: Neither H3.1K27M nor H3.3K27M oncohistone interferes with PRC2 binding to chromatin in DMG cells.
source: Finally, we find that neither H3K27M oncohistone interferes with PRC2 binding to chromatin in DMG cells.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling of SUZ12 and MTF2 (Figure 5A, 5B).

claim: H3K27M oncohistones inhibit PRC2 on chromosomes.
source: These results support a model where H3K27M oncohistones inhibit PRC2 on chromosomes, helping to explain the origin of gliomas during proliferative periods in development and the spectra of secondary mutations in these gliomas.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Histone H3 variants are highly conserved across evolution.
source: Histone H3 variants are highly conserved across evolution, and identical H3.3 histones are produced in both humans and Drosophila (Ahmad and Henikoff, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: Identical H3.3 histones are produced in both humans and Drosophila.
source: Histone H3 variants are highly conserved across evolution, and identical H3.3 histones are produced in both humans and Drosophila (Ahmad and Henikoff, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: Humans have two replication-dependent H3-type histones – H3.1 and H3.2.
source: Humans have two replication-dependent H3-type histones – H3.1 and H3.2 – while Drosophila has only one, which is identical to H3.2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about histone biology.

claim: Drosophila has only one replication-dependent H3-type histone, which is identical to H3.2.
source: Humans have two replication-dependent H3-type histones – H3.1 and H3.2 – while Drosophila has only one, which is identical to H3.2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about histone biology.

claim: Nuclei that overexpress tagged histone H3.2 or H3.3 show broad staining for H3K27 trimethylation at similar levels as untransfected control nuclei.
source: Nuclei that overexpress tagged histone H3.2 or H3.3 show broad staining for H3K27 trimethylation at similar levels as untransfected control nuclei (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1B.

claim: H3.2K27M and H3.3K27M constructs show dramatic reduction of H3K27me3 in Drosophila S2 cells.
source: In contrast, the same constructs with a K27M mutation show dramatic reduction of H3K27me3 (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1B.

claim: Both H3.2 and H3.3 K27M oncohistones can inhibit H3K27 methylation to similar degrees when similarly overexpressed.
source: These results show that both H3.2 and H3.3 K27M oncohistones can inhibit H3K27 methylation to similar degrees, at least when similarly overexpressed.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunofluorescence data in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: A soluble H3K27M tail peptide can inhibit the EZH2 methyltransferase in vitro.
source: A soluble H3K27M tail peptide can inhibit the EZH2 methyltransferase in vitro (Lewis et al., 2013), so we introduced a construct encoding only the histone H3.2 N-terminal tail (residues 1–44) fused to Red Fluorescent Protein (RFP).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: H3K27 trimethylation levels are unaffected in cells expressing either the wild-type histone tail or the K27M histone tail fusion protein.
source: We observed that H3K27 trimethylation levels are unaffected in cells expressing either the wild-type histone tail or the K27M histone tail fusion protein (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1B.

claim: The H3K27M oncohistone must be incorporated into chromatin to block H3K27 trimethylation.
source: Thus, we infer that while the H3K27M oncohistone can block H3K27 trimethylation, it must be incorporated into chromatin to do so.
evidence: This is inferred from the histone tail fusion protein experiments in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Incorporation of H3.1 and H3.2 histones into chromatin is coupled to DNA replication as new nucleosomes are assembled behind replication forks.
source: Incorporation of H3.1 and H3.2 histones into chromatin is coupled to DNA replication as new nucleosomes are assembled behind replication forks (Ahmad and Henikoff, 2002; Tagami et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: Expression of a H3.3K27M mutant histone in developing wing imaginal discs inhibits H3K27 trimethylation and Polycomb-mediated silencing.
source: Expression of a H3.3K27M mutant histone in developing wing imaginal discs inhibits H3K27 trimethylation and Polycomb-mediated silencing (Herz et al., 2014; Ahmad and Spens, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Following proliferation of eye progenitor cells, one last synchronized wave of cell division moves across a disc just posterior to the morphogenetic furrow (MF).
source: Following proliferation of eye progenitor cells, one last synchronized wave of cell division moves across a disc just posterior to the morphogenetic furrow (MF) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila eye development, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The GMR-GAL4 driver produces the GAL4 activator only in the posterior portion of the eye disc.
source: The lateeye-specific GMR-GAL4 driver produces the GAL4 activator only in the posterior portion of the disc, and thus induction of a GAL4-responsive histone transgene will produce the protein only in cells that are destined to go through only one more division before terminally differentiating into photoreceptors (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GMR-GAL4 system, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Expression of either H3.3 or H3.3K27M at late time in eye development had no effect on eye morphology.
source: Expression of either H3.3 or H3.3K27M at this late time in development had no effect on eye morphology (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by adult eye images in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: Eye imaginal discs from wild-type larvae show similar staining of H3K27 trimethylation in both the anterior and posterior differentiating regions.
source: Eye imaginal discs from wild-type larvae show similar staining of H3K27 trimethylation in both the anterior and posterior differentiating regions (Figure 2I), and induction of a wild-type H3.3 transgene had no effect on this pattern (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2I and 2J.

claim: Induction of a wild-type H3.3 transgene had no effect on H3K27 trimethylation pattern in eye discs.
source: Eye imaginal discs from wild-type larvae show similar staining of H3K27 trimethylation in both the anterior and posterior differentiating regions (Figure 2I), and induction of a wild-type H3.3 transgene had no effect on this pattern (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Induction of the H3.3K27M oncohistone dramatically inhibits H3K27 trimethylation posterior to the morphogenetic furrow in the eye disc.
source: In contrast, induction of the H3.3K27M oncohistone dramatically inhibits H3K27 trimethylation posterior to the morphogenetic furrow in the eye disc (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: H3.3K27M expression in arrested cells does not inhibit H3K27 trimethylation.
source: Strikingly, we observed that H3.3K27M expression in these arrested cells does not inhibit H3K27 trimethylation (Figure 2L,M).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2L and quantified in Figure 2M.

claim: The H3.3K27M oncohistone is a potent inhibitor of H3K27 trimethylation, but is only effective in proliferating cells.
source: These experiments demonstrate that the H3.3K27M oncohistone is a potent inhibitor of H3K27 trimethylation, but is only effective in proliferating cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the Drosophila eye disc experiments with p21 co-expression (Figure 2L, 2M).

claim: The genomic distribution of H3.3K27M has been previously mapped in DMG patient-derived cell lines.
source: The genomic distribution of H3.3K27M has been previously mapped in DMG patient-derived cell lines (Piunti et al., 2017); however, the distribution of H3.1K27M was not known.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The distribution of H3.1K27M was not known prior to this study.
source: The genomic distribution of H3.3K27M has been previously mapped in DMG patient-derived cell lines (Piunti et al., 2017); however, the distribution of H3.1K27M was not known.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The monoclonal antibody used to detect the K27M substitution reacts with the mutated residue in both H3.1 and in H3.3 histones.
source: The monoclonal antibody we used to detect the K27M substitution reacts with the mutated residue in both H3.1 and in H3.3 histones (Venneti et al., 2014), and we therefore examined K27M oncohistone abundance and distribution in two H3.3K27M-carrying (SU-DIPG-XIII and SU-DIPG-XVII; 'XIII' and 'XVII') patient-derived cell lines, and in two H3.1K27M-carrying (SU-DIPG-IV and SU-DIPG-XXXVI; 'IV' and 'XXXVI') lines to compare the effects of histone subtypes.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and Western blotting data (Figure 3A).

claim: The K27M epitope is present in all four H3K27M oncohistone DMGs.
source: We first confirmed that the K27M epitope was present in all four H3K27M oncohistone DMGs by Western blotting, with different amounts of oncohistone between lines (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Different amounts of K27M oncohistone are present between DMG cell lines.
source: We first confirmed that the K27M epitope was present in all four H3K27M oncohistone DMGs by Western blotting, with different amounts of oncohistone between lines (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Two high-grade glioma (HGG) cell lines (VUMC and PBT) with wild-type H3.1 and H3.3 genes show no detectable K27M signal.
source: In contrast, two high-grade glioma (HGG) cell lines (VUMC and PBT) with wild-type H3.1 and H3.3 genes show no detectable K27M signal, demonstrating the specificity of the anti-K27M antibody.
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The effects on abundance of H3K27me3 are not related to the amount of K27M oncohistone expressed.
source: The effects on abundance of H3K27me3 are not related to the amount of K27M oncohistone expressed (Figure 3A), but appear related to the oncohistone type.
evidence: This is inferred from Western blotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The effects on abundance of H3K27me3 appear related to the oncohistone type.
source: The effects on abundance of H3K27me3 are not related to the amount of K27M oncohistone expressed (Figure 3A), but appear related to the oncohistone type.
evidence: This is inferred from Western blotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CUT&RUN relies on binding of a specific antibody to chromosomal sites to tether a protein A-micrococcal nuclease (pA-MNase) fusion protein in samples of unfixed cells.
source: CUT&RUN relies on binding of a specific antibody to chromosomal sites to tether a protein A-micrococcal nuclease (pA-MNase) fusion protein in samples of unfixed cells.
evidence: This is a description of the CUT&RUN method.

claim: Abundant nucleosomal fragments are released from both H3.3K27M- and H3.1K27M-bearing cell lines in CUT&RUN reactions.
source: Cleavage at antibody-targeted chromatin can be detected as nucleosomal fragments released from cells after nuclease activation, and we observed abundant fragments released from both H3.3K27M- and H3.1K27M-bearing cell lines (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by capillary electrophoresis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There is no detectable DNA released from VUMC cells in K27M CUT&RUN reactions.
source: In contrast, there is no detectable DNA released from VUMC cells, which express wild-type H3.1 and H3.3 histones, or from cells incubated with a control IgG antibody, indicating that the CUT&RUN reactions specifically cleave chromatin containing K27M oncohistones.
evidence: This is supported by capillary electrophoresis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CUT&RUN reactions specifically cleave chromatin containing K27M oncohistones.
source: In contrast, there is no detectable DNA released from VUMC cells, which express wild-type H3.1 and H3.3 histones, or from cells incubated with a control IgG antibody, indicating that the CUT&RUN reactions specifically cleave chromatin containing K27M oncohistones.
evidence: This is inferred from the capillary electrophoresis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CUT&RUN profiling of the K27M epitope showed moderate signal across the genome in both H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M lines.
source: CUT&RUN profiling of the K27M epitope showed moderate signal across the genome in both H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M lines (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by distribution graphs shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The genome-wide K27M signal is absent in cells lacking K27M oncohistones.
source: This genome-wide signal is absent in cells lacking K27M oncohistones, and thus represents oncohistone that is broadly distributed.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution graphs shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The XIII H3.3K27M line displayed 7,411 distinct K27M peaks.
source: In addition, the XIII H3.3K27M line displayed 7,411 distinct peaks (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by peak calling analysis reported in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Many K27M peaks in H3.3K27M cells correspond to promoters.
source: Notably, many of these peaks correspond to promoters, and overall these promoters are substantially enriched for K27M signal (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: K27M peaks indicate that the H3.3K27M oncohistone is incorporated at sites of active histone turnover, superimposed upon a genome-wide background signal.
source: These peaks indicate that the H3.3K27M oncohistone is incorporated at sites of active histone turnover, superimposed upon a genome-wide background signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the CUT&RUN profiling data showing peaks at promoters (Figure 3E).

claim: 44% of the K27M oncohistone peaks fall precisely at called peaks of H3K4me2.
source: Indeed, 44% of the K27M oncohistone peaks fall precisely at called peaks of H3K4me2 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis reported in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Many K27M peaks coincide with the promoters of actively transcribed genes in DMGs, including SOX2, OLIG2, MYC and GFAP.
source: Many K27M peaks coincide with the promoters of actively transcribed genes in DMGs, including SOX2, OLIG2, MYC and GFAP (Supplementary file 2), and the K27M signal has a moderate correlation (R2 = 0.3) with gene expression measured by RNA-seq in these cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Nagaraja et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by peak analysis in Supplementary file 2 and correlation analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The K27M signal has a moderate correlation (R2 = 0.3) with gene expression measured by RNA-seq in H3.3K27M cells.
source: Many K27M peaks coincide with the promoters of actively transcribed genes in DMGs, including SOX2, OLIG2, MYC and GFAP (Supplementary file 2), and the K27M signal has a moderate correlation (R2 = 0.3) with gene expression measured by RNA-seq in these cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Nagaraja et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: No H3K27M signal is observed in HGG lines with wild-type H3.3 histones.
source: In contrast, no H3K27M signal is observed in HGG lines with wild-type H3.3 histones (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: H3K27M-targeted CUT&RUN released abundant amounts of nucleosome-sized DNA from H3.1K27M-bearing cell lines.
source: Although H3K27M-targeted CUT&RUN released abundant amounts of nucleosome-sized DNA (Figure 3B) and 4–8 million fragments were sequenced and mapped, these reads are uniformly distributed across the genome for each of the two H3.1K27M-bearing cell lines (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by capillary electrophoresis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 4–8 million fragments were sequenced and mapped from H3.1K27M-bearing cell lines.
source: Although H3K27M-targeted CUT&RUN released abundant amounts of nucleosome-sized DNA (Figure 3B) and 4–8 million fragments were sequenced and mapped, these reads are uniformly distributed across the genome for each of the two H3.1K27M-bearing cell lines (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the sequencing data.

claim: K27M reads are uniformly distributed across the genome for each of the two H3.1K27M-bearing cell lines.
source: Although H3K27M-targeted CUT&RUN released abundant amounts of nucleosome-sized DNA (Figure 3B) and 4–8 million fragments were sequenced and mapped, these reads are uniformly distributed across the genome for each of the two H3.1K27M-bearing cell lines (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by distribution graphs shown in Figure 3C.

claim: H3K27M signal did not aggregate into defined peaks in H3.1K27M-bearing cell lines.
source: Additionally, we found that H3K27M signal did not aggregate into defined peaks and was not enriched over promoters (Figure 3E) or over H3K4me2 peaks (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 3E and peak overlap analysis in Supplementary file 1.

claim: H3K27M signal was not enriched over promoters in H3.1K27M-bearing cell lines.
source: Additionally, we found that H3K27M signal did not aggregate into defined peaks and was not enriched over promoters (Figure 3E) or over H3K4me2 peaks (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The distributions of the two oncohistones are consistent with replication-coupled histone deposition for both H3.1 and H3.3 oncohistones, and additional replication-independent deposition of H3.3K27M at active sites.
source: Thus, we conclude that while both H3.1 and H3.3 K27M mutations result in the incorporation of the H3K27M epitope into chromatin, the distributions of the two oncohistones are consistent with replication-coupled histone deposition for both H3.1 and H3.3 oncohistones, and additional replication-independent deposition of H3.3K27M at active sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the CUT&RUN profiling data showing different distribution patterns (Figure 3C, 3E).

claim: The widespread K27M signal in both H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M lines is present in H3K27me3 domains.
source: Finally, we noted that the widespread K27M signal in both H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M lines is present in H3K27me3 domains (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The K27M epitope inhibits the H3K27 methyltransferase EZH2 in vitro.
source: The K27M epitope inhibits the H3K27 methyltransferase EZH2 in vitro, in cell culture, and in H3.3K27M-bearing cell lines (Castel et al., 2015; Funato and Tabar, 2018; Mohammad and Helin, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The K27M epitope inhibits the H3K27 methyltransferase EZH2 in cell culture.
source: The K27M epitope inhibits the H3K27 methyltransferase EZH2 in vitro, in cell culture, and in H3.3K27M-bearing cell lines (Castel et al., 2015; Funato and Tabar, 2018; Mohammad and Helin, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The K27M epitope inhibits the H3K27 methyltransferase EZH2 in H3.3K27M-bearing cell lines.
source: The K27M epitope inhibits the H3K27 methyltransferase EZH2 in vitro, in cell culture, and in H3.3K27M-bearing cell lines (Castel et al., 2015; Funato and Tabar, 2018; Mohammad and Helin, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Western blotting for H3K27me3 shows very low levels of this histone modification in both H3.3 and H3.1 K27M mutant cells.
source: Indeed, western blotting for H3K27me3 shows very low levels of this histone modification in both H3.3 and H3.1 K27M mutant cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A fixed ratio of Drosophila S2 cells to human cells was used as a spike-in control for H3K27me3 CUT&RUN.
source: Since the H3K27me3 epitope is conserved between Drosophila and humans, we used a fixed ratio of Drosophila S2 cells to human cells as a spike-in control.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The H3K27me3 epitope is conserved between Drosophila and humans.
source: Since the H3K27me3 epitope is conserved between Drosophila and humans, we used a fixed ratio of Drosophila S2 cells to human cells as a spike-in control.
evidence: This is established knowledge about histone modifications.

claim: Normalization of human read counts by Drosophila read counts allows direct comparison between samples.
source: Normalization of human read counts by Drosophila read counts then allows direct comparison between samples.
evidence: This is a description of the normalization method.

claim: The validity of the spike-in approach is demonstrated by the linear relationship between read counts when varying the ratio of Drosophila and human cells in a H3K27me3 CUT&RUN reaction.
source: The validity of this spike-in approach is demonstrated by the linear relationship between read counts when varying the ratio of Drosophila and human cells in a H3K27me3 CUT&RUN reaction (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Track browsing showed high signals for H3K27me3 in H3.3K27M cells at canonical silenced domains, such as the HOXD locus.
source: Track browsing showed high signals for H3K27me3 in H3.3K27M cells at canonical silenced domains, such as the HOXD locus (Figure 3C), as previous studies have also shown (Piunti et al., 2017; Harutyunyan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by genome browser tracks shown in Figure 3C and cited literature.

claim: H3K27me3 is greatly reduced at the HOXD locus in H3.1K27M-bearing cells.
source: However, it is apparent that H3K27me3 is greatly reduced at the HOXD locus in H3.1K27M-bearing cells.
evidence: This is supported by genome browser tracks shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Many methylation domains present in VUMC cells are lacking in H3.3K27M cells.
source: Strikingly, it is also apparent that many methylation domains present in VUMC cells are lacking in H3.3K27M cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the genome browser tracks and clustering analysis (Figure 4A).

claim: Unsupervised clustering of variable H3K27me3 domains generated four major groups.
source: To analyze differences between cell lines more thoroughly, we defined differentially methylated chromatin domains between the H3.1K27M (SU-DIPG-IV), H3.3K27M (SU-DIPG-XIII), and histone wild-type (VUMC-10) glioma lines. Unsupervised clustering of these variable H3K27me3 domains generated four major groups (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Clusters I-II comprise 17,534 domains which are present in VUMC cells but absent in H3.3K27M cells.
source: The largest clusters (Clusters I-II) comprise 17,534 domains which are present in VUMC cells but absent in H3.3K27M cells, including numerous tissue-specific transcription factors.
evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cluster III includes 156 domains that are found both in VUMC and in H3.3K27M cells.
source: Cluster III includes 156 domains that are found both in VUMC and in H3.3K27M cells, and encompass genes that are typically silenced in many cell types, including those for the CDKN2A cell cycle inhibitor, the WT1 tumor suppressor, and the HOXD transcription factors.
evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cluster IV contains 1,380 domains that are absent in VUMC cells but present in H3.3K27M cells.
source: Finally, cluster IV contains 1,380 domains that are absent in VUMC cells but present in H3.3K27M cells, including many critical regulators of developmental processes (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 4A and gene ontology analysis in Supplementary file 4.

claim: H3.3K27M cells are distinguished from other high-grade gliomas by the lack of a large number of H3K27me3 domains across the genome.
source: Thus, while H3.3K27M cells do have some H3K27 methylated domains, they are distinguished from other high-grade gliomas by the lack of a large number of H3K27me3 domains across the genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the clustering analysis showing Clusters I and II are absent in H3.3K27M cells (Figure 4A).

claim: The reduction in domain numbers but not in H3K27 trimethylation levels across those domains implies that EZH2 enzyme remains active in H3.3K27M-bearing cells.
source: The reduction in domain numbers but not in H3K27 trimethylation levels across those domains (Figure 4) implies that EZH2 enzyme remains active in H3.3K27M-bearing cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DMG cells express transcription factors of both pluripotency and differentiated cell types.
source: Indeed, DMG cells do express transcription factors of both pluripotency and differentiated cell types, suggesting developmental similarity to both stem cells and to differentiated cells (Filbin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: 5,259 domains (21.3%) of the 24,733 domains found in U5 NSCs are found in VUMC cells.
source: We found that 5,259 domains (21.3%) of the 24,733 domains found in U5 NSCs are found in VUMC cells, while only 1,287 (5.20%) are shared with H3.3K27M cells.
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis of H3K27me3 domains.

claim: Only 1,287 (5.20%) of U5 NSC H3K27me3 domains are shared with H3.3K27M cells.
source: We found that 5,259 domains (21.3%) of the 24,733 domains found in U5 NSCs are found in VUMC cells, while only 1,287 (5.20%) are shared with H3.3K27M cells.
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis of H3K27me3 domains.

claim: 375 domains (26.8%) of 1,401 domains in H1 ESCs are present in H3.3K27M-bearing cells.
source: In contrast, 375 domains (26.8%) of 1,401 domains in H1 ESCs are present in H3.3K27M-bearing cells.
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis of H3K27me3 domains.

claim: Both H3.3K27M and ES cells are distinctive in lacking H3K27 trimethylation from most Cluster I and II domains.
source: Additionally, both H3.3K27M and ES cells are distinctive in lacking H3K27 trimethylation from most Cluster I and II domains, and thus have a very limited global H3K27me3 profile.
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: H3.3K27M and ES cells have a very limited global H3K27me3 profile.
source: Additionally, both H3.3K27M and ES cells are distinctive in lacking H3K27 trimethylation from most Cluster I and II domains, and thus have a very limited global H3K27me3 profile.
evidence: This is inferred from the heatmap analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Epigenomic changes are much more severe in H3.1K27M cells.
source: Epigenomic changes are much more severe in H3.1K27M cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of H3K27me3 levels between H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M cells.

claim: H3.1K27M cells have very low bulk levels of H3K27 trimethylation, but domains can still be detected.
source: These cells have very low bulk levels of H3K27 trimethylation, but domains can still be detected (Supplementary file 1), and cover many of the same regions found in H3.3K27M cells (Figure 4A, Clusters III and IV).
evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 4A and peak calling in Supplementary file 1.

claim: H3K27 trimethylation in H3.1K27M domains is reduced to 2–10% of the levels in VUMC or H3.3K27M cells.
source: However, spike-in quantitation show that H3K27 trimethylation in these domains is reduced to 2–10% of the levels in VUMC or even in H3.3K27M cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by spike-in normalized CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 5B.

claim: The H3.3K27M and H3.1K27M oncohistones have dramatically different effects on Polycomb-regulated domains.
source: Thus, the H3.3K27M and H3.1K27M oncohistones have dramatically different effects on Polycomb-regulated domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative differences in H3K27me3 levels (Figure 5B).

claim: This quantitative effect appears to be a conserved property of H3K27M mutant histones, as replication-coupled H3.2K27M oncohistones are more potent inhibitors of H3K27 trimethylation than H3.3K27M oncohistones in C. elegans.
source: This quantitative effect appears to be a conserved property of H3K27M mutant histones, as replication-coupled H3.2K27M oncohistones are more potent inhibitors of H3K27 trimethylation than H3.3K27M oncohistones in C. elegans (Delaney et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The two H3.1K27M-bearing cell lines have biallelic deletions of the CDKN2A gene.
source: We further genotyped these cell lines by targeted gene sequencing (Kuo et al., 2020), and identified multiple genetic alterations (Supplementary file 5), including biallelic deletions of the CDKN2A gene in the two H3.1K27M-bearing cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by targeted sequencing data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: The CDKN2A tumor suppressor gene is normally repressed by Polycomb silencing in normal cells.
source: This tumor suppressor gene is normally repressed by Polycomb silencing in normal cells, and suggests that inhibition of H3K27me3 by H3.1K27M requires secondary deletion of the CDKN2A locus for cell survival.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CDKN2A regulation.

claim: Inhibition of H3K27me3 by H3.1K27M requires secondary deletion of the CDKN2A locus for cell survival.
source: This tumor suppressor gene is normally repressed by Polycomb silencing in normal cells, and suggests that inhibition of H3K27me3 by H3.1K27M requires secondary deletion of the CDKN2A locus for cell survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the genotyping data showing CDKN2A deletions in H3.1K27M cells (Supplementary file 5).

claim: The CDKN2A locus is not typically altered in H3.3K27M-bearing cells.
source: In contrast, the CDKN2A locus is not typically altered in H3.3K27M-bearing cells (Piunti et al., 2017; Mohammad and Helin, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: H3K27M oncohistones have been suggested to trap the PRC2 complex on chromatin and inhibit activity of the EZH2 methyltransferase complex.
source: H3K27M oncohistones have been suggested to trap the PRC2 complex on chromatin and inhibit activity of the EZH2 methyltransferase complex (Stafford et al., 2018; Fang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: Similar amounts of SUZ12 and MTF2 proteins are present in all three gliomas (VUMC, H3.3K27M, H3.1K27M).
source: Similar amounts of these proteins are present in all three gliomas (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Thousands of sites for SUZ12 and MTF2 were detected in each glioma line.
source: We detected thousands of sites for each subunit in each line (Supplementary file 1), with high concordance between biological replicates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by peak calling data in Supplementary file 1 and correlation analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no enrichment of SUZ12 or MTF2 at active promoters with the K27M signal in H3.3K27M-bearing cells.
source: This analysis showed no enrichment of SUZ12 or MTF2 at active promoters with the K27M signal in H3.3K27M-bearing cells (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,C.

claim: K27M-defined peaks were not enriched for SUZ12 or MTF2 PRC2 components.
source: Similarly, K27M-defined peaks were not enriched for these PRC2 components (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: In both the VUMC and H3.3K27M glioma lines, H3K27me3 domains are co-occupied by PRC2.
source: Thus, in both the VUMC and H3.3K27M glioma lines, H3K27me3 domains are co-occupied by PRC2.
evidence: This is inferred from the CUT&RUN profiling data showing SUZ12 and MTF2 enrichment at H3K27me3 domains (Figure 5A, 5B).

claim: H3.1K27M gliomas have dramatically reduced levels of H3K27me3 in domains, but those domains continue to be enriched for both SUZ12 and MTF2 proteins.
source: While H3.1K27M gliomas have dramatically reduced levels of H3K27me3 in domains, we find that those domains continue to be enriched for both SUZ12 and MTF2 proteins (Clusters III and IV, Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Similar levels of SUZ12 and substantial levels of MTF2 are present in all three cell lines in Cluster III domains.
source: We compared the spike-normalized levels of these proteins across Cluster III sites, which are H3K27me3 domains in all three cell lines, and found similar levels of SUZ12 and substantial levels of MTF2 in all three cell lines in these domains (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Polycomb proteins are correctly targeted in both H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M cells.
source: These results imply that Polycomb proteins are correctly targeted in both H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M cells, but PRC2 must be strongly inhibited in H3.1K27M cells to account for their low H3K27me3 signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the CUT&RUN profiling data showing PRC2 enrichment at domains (Figure 5A, 5B).

claim: PRC2 must be strongly inhibited in H3.1K27M cells to account for their low H3K27me3 signal.
source: These results imply that Polycomb proteins are correctly targeted in both H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M cells, but PRC2 must be strongly inhibited in H3.1K27M cells to account for their low H3K27me3 signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of PRC2 binding and low H3K27me3 levels in H3.1K27M cells (Figure 5B).

claim: Replication-coupled and -independent mechanisms of H3 variant deposition were first demonstrated almost two decades ago.
source: Replication-coupled and -independent mechanisms of H3 variant deposition were first demonstrated almost two decades ago (Ahmad and Henikoff, 2002) but the roles of these different deposition mechanisms in H3.1-and H3.3-mutant gliomagenesis are not known.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: The roles of different deposition mechanisms in H3.1-and H3.3-mutant gliomagenesis are not known.
source: Replication-coupled and -independent mechanisms of H3 variant deposition were first demonstrated almost two decades ago (Ahmad and Henikoff, 2002) but the roles of these different deposition mechanisms in H3.1-and H3.3-mutant gliomagenesis are not known.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Previous reports for the localization of H3.1K27M have been contradictory, identifying accumulation at active promoters or more broadly throughout the genome.
source: Previous reports for the localization of H3.1K27M have been contradictory, identifying accumulation at active promoters (Piunti et al., 2017) or more broadly throughout the genome (Nagaraja et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of conflicting findings in cited literature.

claim: H3.1K27M is deposited throughout the genome, consistent with replication-coupled deposition of H3.1.
source: Our results confirm that H3.1K27M is deposited throughout the genome, consistent with replication-coupled deposition of H3.1, while H3.3K27M accumulates primarily at sites of histone turnover but also at low levels genome-wide, probably through replication-coupled deposition.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling data (Figure 3C, 3E).

claim: H3.3K27M accumulates primarily at sites of histone turnover but also at low levels genome-wide, probably through replication-coupled deposition.
source: Our results confirm that H3.1K27M is deposited throughout the genome, consistent with replication-coupled deposition of H3.1, while H3.3K27M accumulates primarily at sites of histone turnover but also at low levels genome-wide, probably through replication-coupled deposition.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling data (Figure 3C, 3E).

claim: H3K27me3 is much lower in H3.1K27M- than in H3.3K27M-bearing cells.
source: Furthermore, quantitative profiling demonstrates that H3K27me3 is much lower in H3.1K27M- than in H3.3K27M-bearing cells, although neither the H3.1K27M nor H3.3K27M oncohistones appear to trap or prevent PRC2 binding to chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by spike-in normalized CUT&RUN data (Figure 5B).

claim: Neither the H3.1K27M nor H3.3K27M oncohistones appear to trap or prevent PRC2 binding to chromatin.
source: Furthermore, quantitative profiling demonstrates that H3K27me3 is much lower in H3.1K27M- than in H3.3K27M-bearing cells, although neither the H3.1K27M nor H3.3K27M oncohistones appear to trap or prevent PRC2 binding to chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling of SUZ12 and MTF2 (Figure 5A, 5B).

claim: Competing models have suggested that H3K27M oncohistones sequester or poison PRC2.
source: Competing models have suggested that H3K27M oncohistones sequester (Fang et al., 2018) or poison (Lee et al., 2019) PRC2.
evidence: This is a summary of competing hypotheses from cited literature.

claim: It has been suggested that H3K27M effects on PRC2 occur either on chromatin or in solution.
source: Further, it has been suggested that these effects occur either on chromatin or in solution (Nagaraja et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of hypotheses from cited literature.

claim: PRC2 components in DMG cells do not coincide with the bulk of K27M oncohistones in these cells.
source: However, PRC2 components in DMG cells do not coincide with the bulk of K27M oncohistones in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling data (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: The K27M epitope only inhibits H3K27 trimethylation on chromatin in vivo.
source: We have demonstrated that the K27M epitope only inhibits H3K27 trimethylation on chromatin in vivo, supporting the idea that these oncohistones inhibit chromatin-bound PRC2 complexes.
evidence: This is supported by Drosophila experiments with histone tail constructs (Figure 1A, 1B).

claim: EZH2 methylates itself, and this automethylation is required for full catalytic activity.
source: A possible mechanism comes from recent reports showing that EZH2 methylates itself, and that this automethylation is required for full catalytic activity (Lee et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: H3K27M blocks EZH2 automethylation.
source: These studies also showed that H3K27M blocks EZH2 automethylation, and might contribute to the dominant effect of H3K27M mutations.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: H3K27M oncohistones inhibit the EZH2 methyltransferase at its chromatin-binding sites within Polycomb-regulated domains.
source: Our results imply that H3K27M oncohistones inhibit the EZH2 methyltransferase at its chromatin-binding sites within pPolycomb-regulated domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing PRC2 binding at domains with low H3K27me3 (Figure 5A, 5B).

claim: A critical time for maintaining epigenomic patterns is during S phase of the cell cycle, when histone modifications must be established on newly assembled nucleosomes behind the replication fork.
source: A critical time for maintaining epigenomic patterns is during S phase of the cell cycle, when histone modifications must be established on newly assembled nucleosomes behind the replication fork (Alabert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: H3K27M oncohistones inhibit H3K27 trimethylation only in proliferating cells.
source: It is striking that H3K27M oncohistones inhibit H3K27 trimethylation only in proliferating cells (Chan et al., 2013; Nagaraja et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and experimental data in Drosophila (Figure 2L, 2M).

claim: Existing H3K27me3 levels generally remain stable in the absence of DNA replication.
source: Existing H3K27me3 levels generally remain stable in the absence of DNA replication (Jadhav et al., 2020), thus EZH2 activity is only needed in cycling cells.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: EZH2 activity is only needed in cycling cells.
source: Existing H3K27me3 levels generally remain stable in the absence of DNA replication (Jadhav et al., 2020), thus EZH2 activity is only needed in cycling cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature about H3K27me3 stability.

claim: New H3K27M oncohistones deposited behind the replication fork inhibit the EZH2 methyltransferase, thereby blocking re-establishment of H3K27me3 domains.
source: Perhaps new H3K27M oncohistones deposited behind the replication fork inhibit the EZH2 methyltransferase, thereby blocking re-establishment of H3K27me3 domains.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Only H3K27M oncohistones that undergo replication-coupled deposition near the sites of PRC2 recruitment are toxic to EZH2 activity.
source: In this model, only H3K27M oncohistones that undergo replication-coupled deposition near the sites of PRC2 recruitment are toxic to EZH2 activity.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: As H3.1K27M oncohistones are deposited throughout the genome, PRC2 poisoning in these cells eliminates H3K27 trimethylation genome-wide.
source: As H3.1K27M oncohistones are deposited throughout the genome, PRC2 poisoning in these cells eliminates H3K27 trimethylation genome-wide.
evidence: This is inferred from the CUT&RUN profiling data showing uniform H3.1K27M distribution and very low H3K27me3 (Figure 3C, Figure 5B).

claim: The less potent effect of H3.3K27M oncohistones on H3K27 trimethylation in DMG cells may be due to the smaller fraction of H3.3K27M oncohistones that undergo replication-coupled deposition.
source: In contrast, the less potent effect of H3.3K27M oncohistones on H3K27 trimethylation in DMG cells may be due to the smaller fraction of H3.3K27M oncohistones that undergo replication-coupled deposition, as most of this oncohistone is sequestered at active promoters far from H3K27me3 domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the CUT&RUN profiling data showing H3.3K27M enrichment at promoters (Figure 3E).

claim: Most H3.3K27M oncohistone is sequestered at active promoters far from H3K27me3 domains.
source: In contrast, the less potent effect of H3.3K27M oncohistones on H3K27 trimethylation in DMG cells may be due to the smaller fraction of H3.3K27M oncohistones that undergo replication-coupled deposition, as most of this oncohistone is sequestered at active promoters far from H3K27me3 domains.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN profiling data showing H3.3K27M enrichment at promoters (Figure 3E) and lack of co-localization with PRC2 (Figure 5A).

claim: Human histone H3.3 localize over replication foci in early-S-phase cells.
source: The finding that human histone H3.3 localize over replication foci in early-S-phase cells (Ray-Gallet et al., 2011; Clément et al., 2018) is consistent with our model.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Only H3K27M oncohistones deposited during DNA replication are toxic to EZH2 activity.
source: That only H3K27M oncohistones deposited during DNA replication are toxic to EZH2 activity also explains why particular secondary mutations are associated with either H3.1K27M- or H3.3K27M-bearing gliomas.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on the experimental findings.

claim: H3.3K27M but not H3.1K27M gliomas have a significantly increased frequency of ATRX mutations.
source: For example, H3.3K27M but not H3.1K27M gliomas have a significantly increased frequency of ATRX mutations (Khuong-Quang et al., 2012; Mackay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: ATRX is a chromatin remodeler involved in alternative telomere lengthening pathways in some cells.
source: ATRX is a chromatin remodeler involved in alternative telomere lengthening pathways in some cells (Heaphy et al., 2011), but also mediates replication-independent histone deposition (Goldberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: ATRX mediates replication-independent histone deposition.
source: ATRX is a chromatin remodeler involved in alternative telomere lengthening pathways in some cells (Heaphy et al., 2011), but also mediates replication-independent histone deposition (Goldberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: ATRX mutations may enhance the amount of H3.3K27M oncohistones deposited during DNA replication, thereby increasing inhibitory effects on H3K27 trimethylation.
source: Thus, we expect that ATRX mutations may enhance the amount of H3.3K27M oncohistones deposited during DNA replication, thereby increasing inhibitory effects on H3K27 trimethylation.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on the role of ATRX in histone deposition.

claim: CDKN2A loss in H3.1K27M-bearing cells suggests that this oncohistone requires different secondary mutations to compensate for the loss of Polycomb silencing at tumor suppressor genes.
source: Similarly, CDKN2A loss in H3.1K27M-bearing cells suggests that this oncohistone requires different secondary mutations to compensate for the loss of Polycomb silencing at tumor suppressor genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the genotyping data showing CDKN2A deletions in H3.1K27M cells (Supplementary file 5).

claim: Such a dependency would explain why H3.1K27M mutations are more rare than H3.3 ones.
source: Such a dependency would explain why H3.1K27M mutations are more rare than H3.3 ones.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on the requirement for secondary mutations.

claim: H3.1 and H3.3 oncohistones may confer distinct cellular sensitivities to chromatin modification inhibitors.
source: A therapeutic corollary is that H3.1 and H3.3 oncohistones may confer distinct cellular sensitivities to chromatin modification inhibitors, either by affecting chromatin silencing or by affecting histone deposition pathways, thereby reshaping epigenomic landscapes.
evidence: This is a proposed therapeutic implication based on the experimental findings.
